what: ADR log is TSV with printable-binary encoded field values
why: Two decisions, one record, because the second only makes sense given the first.¶¶(1) The log is TSV, not NDJSON. A formats escaping burden is the size of its forbidden-character set. TSV forbids exactly three characters: TAB, CR, LF. NDJSON forbids those plus the double quote and the backslash. Every forbidden character must be encoded into a glyph, so a smaller forbidden set means more of the text survives literally -- and literal text is text that rg finds and an indexer indexes. Under NDJSON we would mangle every quote and backslash in the corpus. Under TSV we mangle nothing a human would type. Smaller records are a real but secondary benefit.¶¶(2) Field values are printable-binary encoded. The convenience argument is that prose keeps its linebreaks, markdown and quotes inside a one-line record. The real argument is correctness: the encoder emits no TAB, no CR and no LF across the entire 256-byte input domain, which makes "an agent botched the escaping and corrupted the log" INEXPRESSIBLE rather than merely unlikely. Botched escaping is precisely the class of error a hurried LLM produces, and this log will be written mostly by LLMs. Same move sigil made when it dropped std.json for a parser whose valid inputs cannot reach the dangerous paths.¶¶The pipe character is deliberately withheld from the preserve set so it can serve as an unambiguous sub-delimiter inside multi-valued fields. Without that exclusion, a path containing a pipe would silently split into two paths.¶¶DO NOT pass -n/--crlf to the encoder. It preserves literal newlines, which would put a raw newline inside a record and destroy the one-record-per-line invariant the whole format rests on. It looks like a harmless legibility upgrade. It is the exact fence this record exists to guard.
alternatives: NDJSON with ordinary JSON string escaping -- rejected. It works, but it puts the escaping burden on the writer, and the writer is usually an LLM. It also forces the quote and backslash to be mangled, which is what broke searchability in the first draft.¶¶Plain unencoded TSV -- rejected. Any tab or newline pasted into a why field silently corrupts the record, and prose is exactly where a pasted newline is likely.¶¶One numbered Markdown file per decision, the classic ADR layout -- rejected. Concurrent agents collide on the next index, and per-file granularity makes the path-matching retrieval hook far more expensive than scanning one file.¶¶Bare printable-binary -s, without the -P preserve set -- rejected after measurement. It re-maps the hyphen to a glyph, so rg "printable-binary" against the log returned ZERO hits. A search that finds nothing is indistinguishable from "no such decision was ever recorded", which is the worst possible failure mode for a Chestertons Fence system.
how: Encode every field with:¶¶    printable-binary -s -P (the preserve set: all printable ASCII punctuation except the pipe)¶¶Decode with printable-binary -d. Join fields with a literal TAB, records with a literal LF, and multi-valued fields with a literal pipe.¶¶To search, encode the needle with the same contract and rg for that. Under the current contract it is a no-op for ordinary prose, but it stays correct if the preserve set is ever narrowed.¶¶Verified exhaustively on 2026-07-28 over all 256 byte values: zero bytes encode to TAB, CR or LF; byte 0x7C never survives literally; roundtrip is byte-identical. The domain is finite, so it was exhausted rather than argued about.
